name: September 1770 Great Aurora

phenomena.details: Modelled minimum Dst ~ -1300 nT (Ebihara et al. 2017), based on red aurora at ~24 degrees magnetic latitude over ~9 nights.
Inferred large X-class flare; no photometric record.

impacts.description: Red aurora visible from Japan (Kyoto, ~24° magnetic latitude) for nine consecutive nights; described in dozens of samurai diaries and official records as a 'red flames across the sky'.

Widely recorded across East Asia, including a vivid red-aurora painting in the Japanese manuscript 'Seikai' (Understanding of the Stars), held by the Matsusaka City Museum of History and Folklore, which has been used to reconstruct the storm's geometry over Kyoto. These records provide critical calibration for historical geomagnetic storm intensity estimates.

papers.title: Long-lasting extreme magnetic storm activities in 1770 found in historical documents
papers.authors: Hayakawa, H., Ebihara, Y., Willis, D. M., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Compiled 111 East Asian historical records of aurora visible for ~9 nights at magnetic latitudes as low as ~24 degrees, indicating a storm rivalling or exceeding the Carrington Event.

papers.title: Inclined zenith aurora over Kyoto on 17 September 1770: Graphical evidence of extreme magnetic storm
papers.keyFinding: Used the red-aurora painting in the 'Seikai' manuscript to reconstruct the auroral geometry over Kyoto, concluding the storm was comparable to or larger than the 1859 Carrington event.

papers.title: Possible cause of extremely bright aurora witnessed in East Asia on 17 September 1770
papers.authors: Ebihara, Y., Hayakawa, H., Iwahashi, K., et al.
papers.keyFinding: Modelled the auroral emission and inferred a minimum Dst of roughly -1300 nT (model-dependent), potentially exceeding the Carrington event.

summary: A geomagnetic storm in September 1770 produced aurora visible across East Asia for nine consecutive nights, down to ~24 degrees magnetic latitude, and is famously depicted in the Japanese 'Seikai' manuscript - modelled as a storm of at least Carrington-class intensity.
description: Contemporary East Asian records - including samurai diaries, domain reports, and astronomical logs - describe vivid red aurora that persisted for nine nights starting on September 17, 1770, visible from locations near 24 degrees magnetic latitude. Modern analysis by Hayakawa et al. (2017) compiled 111 historical sources, and a striking red-aurora painting in the Japanese manuscript 'Seikai' was used by Kataoka and Iwahashi (2017) to reconstruct the display over Kyoto. Modelling of the auroral emission and oval by Ebihara et al. (2017) indicates a storm of at least Carrington-class intensity. The event occurred near the maximum of Solar Cycle 2, and the nine-day duration of visible aurora indicates sustained extreme geomagnetic disturbance, probably from multiple CME arrivals.
